summary: Orbit Academy is a browser game that puts students in command of a four-person lunar or Martian outpost. Over 12 rounds, players balance oxygen, water, food, power, radiation protection and scientific research. Limited supplies and engineering actions force meaningful choices: growing food consumes water and electricity, while storm shelter protects the crew but pauses research. Before each round, a forecast shows the consequences of the current plan. Mission journals and downloadable reports help students explain what happened and improve their next strategy. NASA educational resources inform the engineering concepts; transparent, simplified game values keep the experience accessible to younger learners.“We are [AASTRA]. Our project, Orbit Academy, turns space engineering into decisions students can play. Command a Moon or Mars outpost. Balance air, water, food and power while protecting the crew from radiation. Forecasts reveal each trade-off before the next round. NASA resources inspire the concepts; game values are simplified. Students replay, compare strategies and explain what kept their crew alive.”
details:
Detailed Project Description
### The challenge
Keeping an outpost alive is a systems-engineering problem. A decision that helps one subsystem can strain another. Space-themed learning tools can hide these relationships behind overly simple resource counters or overwhelm learners with operational detail. Orbit Academy makes a small set of important dependencies visible and playable.

### How it works
Students choose a lunar or Martian outpost and manage four astronauts through 12 mission rounds. The goal is to keep crew health above zero while collecting at least 30 science points. Five meters show energy, oxygen, water, food and crew health. Finite supplies and two engineering actions per round limit what can be built.

Players can add solar arrays, water recyclers, oxygen generators and regolith shielding, or open reserve crates. They can switch greenhouse lighting and research on or off and move the crew into a storm shelter. These decisions have explicit costs: life support uses power, oxygen generation uses water, and food production needs both water and electricity. Sheltering reduces radiation damage but pauses research.

Scheduled shadow, dust and solar particle events change the operating conditions. The forecast shows the next resource state before the student commits. A mission journal then records what happened. Success and failure debriefs invite learners to explain their choices, and a downloadable report supports classroom discussion.

### What makes the approach useful
The forecast makes an invisible dependency immediately observable. Students can change one switch, compare the outcome and explain the trade-off. The same deterministic event schedule supports repeatable experiments between strategies. The science objective also creates a reason to do more than simply conserve everything.

### Implementation
The prototype uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A separate simulation engine calculates state transitions; the interface handles controls, forecasts, learning panels and reports. Browser-local storage preserves progress when available. The downloaded game needs no server, API key or software installation. The interface adapts to smaller screens and offers labelled, keyboard-operable controls and reduced-motion support.

### Evidence and limitations
Seven automated engine tests check purchase limits, forecast purity, shelter effects, brownouts and shortages, successful Moon and Mars strategies, mission failure and the science objective. These tests establish internal behavior, not scientific realism or classroom effectiveness. Interactive browser verification has not been completed in this environment. No student study or measured learning improvement is claimed.

The numerical values are invented training units, not operational NASA specifications. Rounds are not Earth days or Martian sols. Crop growth and radiation effects are compressed, and carbon dioxide removal, pressure, thermal control and equipment reliability are not simulated. The result is a teaching prototype rather than a mission-planning or medical model.

### Intended impact and next steps
The learning goal is for students to describe dependencies, justify a safety decision and use evidence to improve a plan. Proposed next steps are classroom pilots, teacher feedback, assessment questions and more realistic scenarios. These are planned improvements, not completed results.
